question: ATS 7.2.2.D.3 limits turns-ratio results to a deviation of not more than:
choices: 0.1% for every transformer
one-half percent from the adjacent coils or the calculated ratio
2% of the factory winding resistance
5% of nameplate impedance
explanation: One-half percent, from the adjacent coils or from the calculated ratio. The 0.1% figure is the revenue VT ratio screen in 7.10.2, not a power-transformer TTR limit. Two percent is winding resistance.

question: On a liquid-filled power transformer, turns ratio is performed:
choices: Only on the as-found tap, to save time
At all tap positions
Only if excitation current already failed
Only on the middle phase
explanation: ATS 7.2.2.B.3 says perform turns-ratio tests at all tap positions. A bad extreme tap will not show up on the nameplate tap alone.

question: ATS 7.2.2.D.6 describes the usual excitation-current pattern on a three-legged core as:
choices: Three identical readings
Two similar readings and one lower reading
One very high reading and two zeros
A reading that must match the DLRO within 2%
explanation: Two similar currents and one lower current is the pattern the paragraph calls typical for a three-legged core. The test should still match the pattern for that specific core. A single phase many times higher than the others is not that pattern.

question: Before you compare a liquid-filled transformer power factor with Table 100.3, ATS 7.2.2.D.4 says the value is:
choices: Left at the temperature of the test
Corrected to 20 °C
Corrected to 40 °C like a motor PI
Multiplied by the turns ratio
explanation: Maximum power-factor or dissipation-factor values are corrected to 20 °C and then compared with the manufacturer or, if none, Table 100.3. Distribution transformers are compared with previous results rather than forced into the power-transformer cap.

question: Manufacturer published insulation-resistance values exist and they disagree with Table 100.5. What does the ATS pattern require?
choices: Always use the NETA table; it is the law
Use the manufacturer's data; the NETA table is for the absence of that data
Average the two numbers
Use whichever is lower, always
explanation: The insulation paragraphs are written 'in accordance with manufacturer's published data. In the absence of manufacturer's data, use Table…'. When the manufacturer has spoken, that data is the screen. The table is the fallback.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.2.2.D.2 (and the same 'in the absence' pattern throughout Section 7)

question: Mineral-oil power transformers, power factor at 20 °C, when you have no manufacturer limit. Which pair matches the books?
choices: ATS-2025 Table 100.3 maximum 0.5%; MTS-2023 Table 100.3 oil maximum 1.0%
Both books use 0.5%
ATS uses 2.0% and MTS uses 0.5%
Neither book states a number; only the Doble set does
explanation: Acceptance Table 100.3 in ATS-2025 caps mineral-oil power transformers, regulators, and reactors at 0.5% (natural ester in that row is 1.0%). Maintenance Table 100.3 in MTS-2023 lists oil maximum 1.0% for power transformers and 2.0% for distribution transformers and apparatus. Do not file an acceptance report against the maintenance column.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 Table 100.3; ANSI/NETA MTS-2023 Table 100.3

question: Bushing capacitance has moved 7% from the nameplate. ATS 7.2.2.D.5 says:
choices: Acceptable; the screen is 50%
Investigate; capacitance is investigated above a 5% departure, and power factor above a 50% departure
Investigate only if hot-collar watts are under 0.1
Ignore capacitance; only oil power factor matters
explanation: Investigate bushing power factor more than 50% off nameplate, capacitance more than 5% off nameplate, and hot-collar results above 0.1 W. Seven percent capacitance is over the 5% screen even if the power-factor change is still small.

question: ATS Table 100.13 lists SF6 purity greater than 98.5% by volume for pure SF6. A fair use of that table is:
choices: Apply 98.5% to any SF6/N2 mixture without looking at the OEM
Treat it as a field guide for pure SF6, and still compare with the manufacturer; mixed gases follow the manufacturer
Ignore purity if moisture is under 200 ppmv
The table is only a lab test and has no field note
explanation: The table is derived for technical-grade pure SF6 and the notes say field results should be compared with the manufacturer's literature, and mixed gases refer to the manufacturer. Moisture, SO2, and decomposition products are separate rows, not substitutes for purity.

question: Core insulation resistance, ATS 7.2.2.D.11, shall be comparable to factory but not less than:
choices: 500 MΩ at 500 V DC
100 MΩ at 1000 V DC
1 MΩ at 500 V DC
5000 MΩ at 10 kV
explanation: Not less than 500 MΩ at 500 V DC, and comparable to the factory value. If the intentional core ground is still connected, a megger reads the bond, near zero, and you have not performed this test.

question: New mineral oil in new equipment, 69 kV and below, ATS Table 100.4.1. Which set matches the table?
choices: D1816 1 mm gap minimum 25 kV, water maximum 20 ppm, power factor at 25 °C maximum 0.05%
D1816 1 mm gap minimum 35 kV, water maximum 5 ppm, power factor 0.5%
D877 minimum 10 kV only; water is not listed
Neutralization number maximum 0.30 mg KOH/g
explanation: For ≤69 kV the table lists D1816 1 mm minimum 25 kV, 2 mm minimum 45 kV, water 20 ppm, D924 power factor at 25 °C 0.05%, and neutralization number 0.03 mg KOH/g. The 35 kV / 10 ppm column is the ≥230 kV class. Do not slide into the next voltage column.

question: Three-phase equivalent leakage reactance differs from nameplate by 4%. ATS 7.2.2.D.10 says:
choices: Acceptable; the screen is 10%
Investigate; the screen is more than 3% from nameplate
Ignore it if TTR passed
The test applies only to dry-type units under 500 kVA
explanation: Investigate a three-phase equivalent result more than 3% off nameplate. Each phase should also stay within 3% of the average of the three. A ratio that still passes does not retire a leakage-reactance change; the test is looking for winding movement.

question: New mineral oil, every voltage class in ATS Table 100.4.1, has an interfacial-tension minimum of:
choices: 38 mN/m
100 mN/m
No IFT row
explanation: D971 interfacial tension is 38 mN/m minimum in each voltage column of that new-oil table. Water and dielectric strength do change with voltage class. Do not slide those columns into the IFT number.

question: ATS Table 100.13 lists SF6 decomposition SO2 as:
choices: Less than 5 ppmv
Greater than 98.5%
200 ppmv minimum
10% by volume
explanation: SO2 decomposition products are listed below 5 ppmv. Purity is a different row, above 98.5% by volume. The table is a field guide for pure SF6 and still yields to the manufacturer, especially on gas mixtures.

question: Natural-ester fluid in a power transformer, power factor at 20 °C, no manufacturer limit. Which pair matches the books?
choices: ATS-2025 Table 100.3 maximum 1.0%; MTS-2023 Table 100.3 ester column 3.0%
Both books use 0.5%
ATS uses 3.0% and MTS uses 0.5%
Ester is judged with the mineral-oil 0.5% cap
explanation: Acceptance Table 100.3 puts natural ester in the power-transformer row at 1.0%. The maintenance table’s ester column for power transformers is 3.0%. Mineral-oil numbers are lower. Do not file an acceptance report on the maintenance column.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 Table 100.3; ANSI/NETA MTS-2023 Table 100.3

question: A wye winding’s power-factor test voltage should be held to:
choices: The line-to-line rating
The line-to-ground rating, or a bit under it
10 kV even when that exceeds the winding
The low-voltage bushing BIL
explanation: On a wye winding, keep the power-factor test voltage at or a little under the winding's line-to-ground rating. Do not use the line-to-line rating, and do not go above the winding. Lift the neutral ground strap for the specimen measurement and put it back when you are done. ATS-2025 7.2.2.B.4 is the test method and 7.2.2.D.4 is the corrected result you compare afterward.

question: In the Megger DELTA4000 applications guide, a grounded-specimen test (GST) on a two-winding transformer is the connection that:
choices: Measures only the interwinding insulation
Includes the path from the energized winding to ground
Is a DC megohm test
Ignores capacitance
explanation: GST puts the return through ground, so you see the winding-to-ground insulation (and, depending on guards, the interwinding path). UST is the connection that measures between the leads and leaves the ground path out. The guide draws both.
reference: Megger DELTA4000 applications guide, per manufacturer instructions

question: An ungrounded-specimen test (UST) between HV and LV, with ground acting as a guard, is how you read:
choices: CHL, the insulation between the windings
Only the core ground strap
Oil moisture in ppm
Excitation current
explanation: The DELTA4000 guide shows the UST current as the current through the interwinding insulation, with the ground paths not measured. That is the CHL specimen. It is not a substitute for a dissolved-gas sample.
reference: Megger DELTA4000 applications guide, per manufacturer instructions

question: EPA’s overview of SF6 in electric power systems describes the gas as:
choices: A short-lived greenhouse gas similar to CO2
A potent greenhouse gas that remains in the atmosphere for thousands of years
Harmless to vent because it is inert
A substitute for dissolved-gas analysis
explanation: The 2018 EPA overview calls SF6 highly potent (about 22,800 times CO2 over 100 years in that paper) and long-lived (on the order of 3,200 years). Inert when pure does not mean acceptable to release.
reference: EPA, Overview of SF6 Emissions Sources and Reduction Options in Electric Power Systems (2018)

question: The preferred end of a job on SF6 equipment is:
choices: Vent the compartment, then refill from any cylinder
Recover the gas and keep it in a closed handling cycle
Burn off the remainder
Mix it with air to dilute the greenhouse effect
explanation: Recover the gas and keep it in a closed handling cycle. The EPA emissions overview is aimed at that point: keep SF6 out of the air rather than venting it. Gas that has arced is still recovered, as a contaminated product, not released.
reference: EPA, Overview of SF6 Emissions Sources and Reduction Options in Electric Power Systems (2018)

question: Arcing in SF6 can produce:
choices: Only more pure SF6
Decomposition products, including hydrogen fluoride
Dissolved acetylene in the aluminum tank
A higher turns ratio
explanation: EPA’s SF6 overview notes that faulted gas yields toxic by-products such as hydrofluoric acid. That is why arced gas is handled, not vented and not assumed to be the same as a new cylinder.
reference: EPA, Overview of SF6 Emissions Sources and Reduction Options in Electric Power Systems (2018)

question: A rising power factor as test voltage is raised, with capacitance also up, is read in the DELTA4000 method as a hint of:
choices: A shorted turn only
Moisture, until the factory report says otherwise
A perfect dry winding
An open core ground
explanation: Loss that climbs with voltage, especially with capacitance climbing too, is the moisture pattern the applications guide tells you to investigate. You still correct to 20 °C and you still prefer the factory numbers over a rule of thumb.
reference: Megger DELTA4000 applications guide, per manufacturer instructions; ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.2.2.D.4

question: A DGA shows hydrogen dominant with little acetylene. That pattern is usually associated with:
choices: Partial discharge or corona more than a hard arc
A welded core ground only
Normal nitrogen blanket
A failed turns-ratio test
explanation: Clause 6.2.1 says hydrogen is created primarily by corona partial discharge and by stray gassing. Acetylene is the better marker when the fault is sparking or arcing. One sample is not a life sentence; the guide wants the mix and the trend, and a bad bottle can invent or lose hydrogen.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.2.2.D.15; ref. IEEE C57.104-2019, clause 6.2.1

question: A DGA syringe left open, or a sample poured through air, mostly:
choices: Improves the acetylene reading
Lets fault gases escape and lets air in, so the ppm no longer match the oil in the tank
Is the method IEEE C57.104 prefers
Replaces the power-factor test
explanation: Clause 5.1.4.1 says a leaky syringe or an air-exposed sample loses much of the hydrogen and often gains oxygen and nitrogen. ATS 7.2.2.B.15 takes the sample by ASTM D923 and the chromatogram by IEEE C57.104 or ASTM D3612. An open jar is not that sample.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.2.2.B.15 (sample per ASTM D923); ref. IEEE C57.104-2019, clause 5.1.4.1

question: A mineral-oil DGA shows hydrogen with no acetylene. How is that read?
choices: Proof of an arc
Primarily corona partial discharge or stray gassing, not by itself an arc
A failed turns-ratio test
Water in the sample only
explanation: Hydrogen is the corona and stray-gassing gas, and it can also come from a reaction with galvanized steel. Acetylene is the gas that marks arcing. Hydrogen alone is not that call. ATS 7.2.2.D.15 is the acceptance line that points at the guide.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.2.2.D.15; ref. IEEE C57.104-2019, clause 6.2.1

question: A mineral-oil DGA shows methane, ethane, and ethylene. Those gases come from:
choices: Heating of oil or paper
A CT polarity error
The gauge on the nitrogen bottle only
A VLF withstand
explanation: Those three hydrocarbons are the heating gases. Acetylene is the step up into arcing. The sample is still taken under ASTM D923 and judged under the guide ATS names.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.2.2.B.15 and D.15; ref. IEEE C57.104-2019, clause 6.2.1

question: ATS 7.2.2.B.15 says the insulating-liquid sample for dissolved gas is taken:
choices: In an open coffee can
In accordance with ASTM D923, then analyzed per IEEE C57.104 or ASTM D3612
From the cooling-fan motor only
After the transformer is back in service and still moving oil through an open hose
explanation: D923 is the sampling practice. The chromatogram is IEEE C57.104 or ASTM D3612. Evaluation is clause D.15, still under C57.104. An open container loses the gases the test is for.

question: A dissolved-gas result looks odd, and you wonder whether the sample itself is the problem. What makes a DGA sample useless?
choices: The syringe was too clean
The sample was tied to the wrong equipment, or a main-tank sample was swapped with a tap-changer sample
The oil was mineral oil
The test was run at 60 Hz
explanation: A bad serial number or a swapped bottle assigns the gases to the wrong tank. A load-tap-changer compartment is not the main tank. Fix the identity before anyone diagnoses a fault. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.2.2.D.15; ref. IEEE C57.104-2019, clause 5.1.3.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.2.2.D.15; ref. IEEE C57.104-2019, clause 5.1.3

question: Comparing this year's DGA with earlier ones, which situation is the bigger concern?
choices: A single ppm that outranks the rate of change
More concerning when the levels are rising than when you only have the level itself
Valid only if acetylene is zero
A substitute for a turns-ratio test
explanation: A rising generation rate matters more than one concentration. Two samples a year apart are a weak way to see that rate. ATS still requires the evaluation; it does not let you skip the sample.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.2.2.D.15; ref. IEEE C57.104-2019, clause 6.1.4

question: ATS Table 100.4 lists both D877 and D1816 dielectric breakdown. Why is D1816 preferred for oil from an in-service transformer?
choices: D877 uses round electrodes that ignore water
D1816 responds more to particles and dissolved water
D1816 is only for SF6
D877 is the dissolved-gas method
explanation: D877’s flat disks are the routine check the same clause recommends for new, unprocessed oil going into circuit breakers. D1816’s rounded electrodes react more to the particles and water that show up in transformer oil. ATS 7.2.2.D.14 still grades the liquid against Table 100.4.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.2.2.D.14; ref. IEEE C57.106-2006, clause 5.2.1

question: Which oil test results are especially sensitive to contamination when you sample a transformer for ATS 7.2.2?
choices: Turns ratio, excitation current, and winding resistance
Interfacial tension, dissipation factor, dielectric breakdown, color, water, and neutralization number
CT polarity and relay targets
Jacket thickness and bend radius
explanation: Those six move when the oil is dirty or wet. They are not a substitute for a winding test. ATS runs the matching ASTM methods and compares the numbers with Table 100.4.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.2.2.D.14; ref. IEEE C57.106-2006, clause 4.2

question: ATS 7.2.2.D.12 says to investigate:
choices: Oxygen in the nitrogen blanket
A polarization index of 3.0 on a motor
A shield under 10 ohms per 1000 feet
Zone 1 set to 80 percent of the line
explanation: A nitrogen-blanketed tank is supposed to stay oxygen-free. Oxygen in that gas space means the blanket is not doing its job. Positive pressure on the gauge is the companion check in 7.2.2.A.15.

question: The D877 dielectric breakdown test (disk electrodes) is recommended for:
choices: Routine acceptance of new, unprocessed oil for circuit breakers
Dissolved-gas analysis
Every in-service transformer, in place of D1816
Furans in the paper
explanation: D877 uses flat disk electrodes and is the routine new-oil check that clause names for breakers. Transformer oil that is already in service is where D1816 earns its keep, because it reacts more to particles and water. ATS Table 100.4 is still the acceptance table.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.2.2.D.14; ref. IEEE C57.106-2006, clause 5.2.1 item a)

question: On the ATS insulating-oil list, neutralization number measures:
choices: A measure of acidic components, and of oxidation products in service-aged oil
The water content in ppm
The dielectric breakdown in kilovolts
The interfacial tension
explanation: New oil can carry a little acid from refining. In service the number tracks oxidation. ASTM D974 is the color-indicator titration and D664 is the potentiometric one, which matters when the oil is too dark to see the color change. ATS 7.2.2 lists D974 on the liquid tests.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.2.2.B.14; ref. IEEE C57.106-2006, clause 5.3.4

question: Sweep frequency response on a liquid-filled transformer is optional in ATS 7.2.2, and the result should:
choices: Be compared with the factory trace and with earlier field traces
Replace the turns-ratio test
Be a single number corrected to 20 °C
Match Table 100.11
explanation: SFRA is a shape comparison, not a pass/fail table in that paragraph. It is marked optional. The turns-ratio test is still required, and its limit is a separate line.

question: On an oil sample, the ASTM D1524 visual check looks at:
choices: Color and turbidity, which can show free water or solid contamination
Turns ratio
CT excitation
Relay timing
explanation: A visual exam can tell you the sample deserves a full lab workup. It does not replace dielectric strength, water, or dissolved gas. ATS 7.2.2 lists visual condition as ASTM D1524 on the liquid tests.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.2.2.B.14; ref. IEEE C57.106-2006, clause 5.1.8

question: ATS 7.2.2.C.2 requires cooling fans and pumps on a liquid-filled transformer to:
choices: Operate
Be locked out for the turns-ratio test only, with no functional check
Be removed if the oil power factor passes
Run only during a dissolved-gas sample
explanation: The visual and mechanical test values say the fans and pumps shall operate. A transformer that cannot cool will not stay inside its temperature rating once it is loaded. The check is separate from the oil tests.

question: ATS 7.2.2.C.1 says alarm, control, and trip circuits from temperature, level, pressure-relief, and sudden-pressure devices shall:
choices: Operate at the manufacturer’s specified settings
Be left disconnected
Be tested only with primary current
Replace the dissolved-gas test
explanation: Those devices are the transformer’s own protection. They have to operate within the settings the manufacturer published. A target that never moves is not an accepted alarm.

question: ATS 7.2.2.A.19 says the de-energized tap changer is left:
choices: On the tap the specification calls for
On the highest tap, always
In a mid position with no record
Wherever the TTR leads fit
explanation: The ratio test visits the taps. The as-left position is the one the job specified, not the last tap you happened to test. Record it.

question: ATS 7.2.2.A.14 checks that transformer valves are:
choices: In the correct operating position
All closed, including the radiators, for service
Removed
Used as the oil sample point with no other check
explanation: A radiator valve left shut looks like a cooling failure once the transformer is loaded. The inspection confirms the operating position. It is not a substitute for the oil sample.

question: ATS 7.2.2.A.15 on a gas-blanketed transformer checks that:
choices: Positive pressure is maintained
The blanket is vented before the ratio test
Oxygen is added to sweeten the gas space
The sudden-pressure relay is jumpered
explanation: The gauge should show positive pressure. Losing the blanket lets air in. A later electrical value, D.12, tells you to investigate oxygen in that nitrogen space.

question: ATS 7.2.2.D.19 says transformer heaters:
choices: Shall be operational
Are optional and untested
Replace the space heater on a motor only
Are disconnected if the oil is dry
explanation: Control-cabinet heaters keep moisture off the relays and the mechanism. The test value is that they work. A dry oil sample does not prove the heater.

question: ATS 7.1.1.A.5 checks the switchgear mimic diagram and device labels against:
choices: The drawings
The oil color
IEEE 519 Table 1
The crew leader’s certification card
explanation: A mimic that does not match the one-line will get the wrong breaker racked out. The labels are part of that same visual check.

question: ATS 7.1.1.A.11 says moving current-carrying parts and sliding surfaces in switchgear need:
choices: The lubrication the design calls for
No lubricant, because grease always contaminates insulation
Oil from the transformer tank
A dielectric grease rated for the BIL only
explanation: The inspection verifies appropriate lubrication on those parts. The wrong grease, or none, is a mechanical failure of a disconnect or a shutter. It is not an insulation-resistance test.

question: A soybean-ester transformer has three DGA samples over six months. Hydrogen rises on each one. Ethane is elevated but flat, acetylene isn’t detected, and CO, CO2, methane, and ethylene are steady. What is the best read and next step?
choices: Stray gassing from the ester; no action needed
Possible partial discharge; confirm it, sample sooner, and plan a test
Arcing; de-energize now
Paper overheating; review the loading history and take no further action
explanation: In an ester, hydrogen is the main partial-discharge gas. Stray gassing in soybean and rapeseed esters shows up as ethane, and ethane here is flat, so it doesn’t explain the hydrogen. No acetylene argues against arcing, and steady carbon oxides argue against hot paper. C57.155 also says a natural ester makes roughly a tenth of the discharge gas mineral oil would for the same fault, so a modest rise matters. A rising gas means an active source: confirm it, sample more often, and consider electrical tests.

question: A new soybean-ester transformer’s first-year DGA shows ethane climbing to a few hundred ppm and then leveling off. Other combustible gases stay low and flat, and there is no acetylene. The owner asks if the unit should come out of service. What do you recommend?
choices: Remove it; ethane this high means a thermal fault
Judge it against the mineral-oil C57.104 limits and act on that reading
Drain and replace the fluid to get rid of the ethane
Keep it in service; the ethane fits stray gassing, so trend from here
explanation: Esters with linolenic acid, such as soybean and rapeseed, make ethane by oxidation in normal service. C57.155 notes it can reach several hundred ppm and then level off without the other combustibles rising. A real fault would bring other gases with it. Keep monitoring until ethane stabilizes, then use that as the baseline. Light, oxygen, and heat change the ethane reading, so handle samples carefully. ATS 7.2.2.D.15 names C57.104, which is written for mineral oil.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.2.2.B.15 and D.15; ref. IEEE C57.155-2014, clauses 4.1 and 4.1.1

question: After a through-fault, an ester-filled transformer’s DGA shows new acetylene, along with jumps in hydrogen, methane, ethylene, CO, and CO2. A tech wants to call it paper overheating from the CO2/CO ratio, using mineral-oil rules. What is the better call?
choices: Agree; carbon oxides read the same in ester as in mineral oil, so use that ratio
Treat it as possible arcing; confirm soon and weigh testing or inspection
Ignore it; through-faults always leave some acetylene
Call it stray gassing and keep the normal sampling interval
explanation: New acetylene with hydrogen and hydrocarbons is the arcing pattern in an ester, much as in mineral oil. Carbon oxides come out of an ester in different proportions and rates, and overheated ester makes them on its own, so a mineral-oil ratio can mislead you about the paper. C57.155 warns that arcing can harm the insulation right away. Confirm the result, then choose testing, inspection, or a shorter interval based on how critical the unit is.

question: An ester-filled unit shows CO and CO2 rising fast, along with methane, ethane, and ethylene, and its acid number is up. The lab comment says “cellulose overheating.” What should you check before accepting that?
choices: Whether the ester is overheating; these gases form cooler than mineral oil, and the acid number fits
Nothing; carbon oxides always mean paper
Whether a partial-discharge source is making the hydrocarbons
Whether the sample sat in sunlight, since sunlight is the only source of the carbon oxides in this sample
explanation: Paper alone makes CO and CO2 but few hydrocarbons. Overheated ester makes a lot of carbon oxides, often more than the paper would, plus methane, ethane, and ethylene starting 50 °C to 100 °C below where mineral oil does. Ester pyrolysis also raises acid number, so acid number and ethylene help sort out the source. Either way, review the loading, temperature, and cooling history.

question: ATS 7.8 says a network protector must close when:
choices: Voltage is present on the transformer side only
Both the feeder and the network are dead
The collector bus is grounded
The phasing relay is removed
explanation: The operational test is: close with voltage on the transformer side only, and open when the source feeder breaker opens. That is how the protector keeps a dead feeder from being back-fed by the network. Master and phasing relays are calibrated with a network-protector test set.

question: When the source feeder breaker opens, ATS 7.8 expects the network protector to:
choices: Stay closed and carry station load
Open
Reclose immediately into the dead feeder
Ignore the feeder and trip only on overload
explanation: Opening with the feeder is the back-feed protection. Closing is allowed when the transformer side alone is live. Trip-free operation is tested in the same operational list.

question: ATS 7.4 visual inspection of metal-enclosed busway includes:
choices: Only a megohm test
Orientation for cooling, weep or drain plugs, and the joint shield
A dissolved-gas sample of the bus
A recloser count test
explanation: The bus has to be installed the way the labels say so it can cool, drains have to match the manufacturer, and the joint shield has to be in place. Insulation resistance and the 50 percent connection rule are the electrical half. Segregated-phase and nonsegregated-phase bus are different rows in Table 100.17, so you do not borrow one type’s withstand voltage for the other.

question: A load tap changer differs from a de-energized tap changer because the load tap changer:
choices: Is moved only with the transformer isolated and grounded
Changes taps while the transformer can be in service
Replaces the turns-ratio test
Is tested as a surge arrester
explanation: ATS leaves the de-energized tap on the specified position after the ratio test, and it has a separate section for the load tap changer. You do not operate a de-energized changer with the winding energized. Ratio is still within one-half percent of calculated at the taps you test.

question: Oil that was clear in the syringe and later shows bubbles should be:
choices: Tested anyway; bubbles improve acetylene
Discarded as an air-exposed sample and taken again
Heated on the transformer until the bubbles vanish
Used for a power-factor test of the winding
explanation: IEEE C57.104-2019 clause 5.1.4.1: air in the sample drives hydrogen out and brings oxygen and nitrogen in. ATS 7.2.2.B.15 takes the sample by ASTM D923. A bubbled syringe is not that sample.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.2.2.B.15; ref. IEEE C57.104-2019, clause 5.1.4.1

question: A gas-blanketed transformer will not push oil out of the sample valve into a syringe when:
choices: The tank gauge shows positive pressure
The tank is under vacuum, below atmospheric pressure
The oil is new
The fans are running
explanation: ATS 7.2.2.A.15 is the check that the gas blanket stays at positive pressure. A tank below atmospheric pressure will not push oil out of the sample valve; that part is physics, not a second sentence in the ATS paragraph. Altitude is not the criterion.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.2.2.A.15; engineering fundamentals (a tank under vacuum will not push oil out)

question: ATS 7.20.1 tells you to deal with stored charge in a power capacitor by:
choices: Measuring the internal discharge-resistor resistance
Skipping the resistor measurement after a one-minute wait
Shorting the terminals with a screwdriver as the procedure
Skipping the resistor if the nameplate says 480 V
explanation: ATS 7.20.1 has you measure the internal discharge resistors. It does not give a discharge time. NEC 2023 460.6(A) does: capacitors under Article 460 have to fall to 50 V or less within one minute after they are disconnected. That minute does not replace the resistor measurement, and it does not make the terminals safe to grab. Read the voltage with a meter and ground the terminals before you touch them.

question: ATS 7.12.3 says the load-tap-changer motor and drive must:
choices: Run past the end of travel until the fuse opens
Cut off automatically at the maximum raise and maximum lower positions
Be left shipped with the bracing installed
Replace the de-energized tap changer while the winding is energized
explanation: Automatic cutoff at both ends of travel is a visual and mechanical check, along with liquid level and the operation counter. A de-energized tap changer is not moved with the transformer in service. Ratio limits remain the transformer section’s one-half percent.

question: ATS 7.20.1 electrical tests on a capacitor include:
choices: Capacitance of all terminal combinations and the internal discharge-resistor resistance
Only a turns-ratio test
A recloser count
A fiber attenuation test
explanation: Insulation resistance is also required. ATS 7.20.1 measures the capacitance of the terminal combinations and the internal discharge-resistor resistance. It does not give a discharge time. NEC 2023 460.6(A) does: capacitors under Article 460 have to be down to 50 V or less within one minute of disconnection. The NEC time is not a reason to skip the resistor measurement, and you still prove the terminals are dead with a meter before you touch them.

question: When the manufacturer is silent, mineral-oil power factor at 20 °C for reactors in ATS Table 100.3 is grouped with:
choices: A separate 5 percent limit
Power transformers and regulators, at 0.5 percent
The rotating-machine PI floor
Table 100.11
explanation: The table title is liquid-filled transformers, regulators, and reactors. Mineral oil in that row is 0.5 percent. Natural ester in the same row is 1.0 percent. Do not use the maintenance table’s higher numbers on an acceptance test.

question: NFPA 70B-2026 Table 11.2 schedules insulating-fluid sampling, for conditions 1, 2, and 3, at:
choices: 12, 12, and 6 months
60, 36, and 12 months for the sample itself
Before each use
Only after a failure
explanation: Fluid sampling and the visual inspection are both 12, 12, and 6 months. Many other transformer tests use the longer 60, 36, and 12 month row when the manufacturer is silent. Infrared is not in that longer bucket. It has its own shorter row. The chapter lists dielectric, acidity, water, and dissolved gas for liquid-filled units and does not print the pass numbers.

question: Which test does NFPA 70B-2026 Table 11.3.5 add for a liquid-filled transformer and not for a dry type?
choices: Dissolved-gas analysis, acidity, water, and dielectric tests of the fluid
A turns-ratio test, which liquid-filled units skip
Excitation current, which only dry types receive
A battery ohmic test
explanation: The electrical table is arranged by size and construction and can include insulation resistance, excitation current, power factor, turns ratio, winding and connection resistance, and partial discharge. Liquid-filled units add the fluid tests. Dry types do not get a dissolved-gas sample. No fluid limit is printed in the chapter.

question: A dry-type transformer maintenance electrical list in NFPA 70B-2026 can include insulation resistance, excitation, power factor, and turns ratio. It does not include:
choices: A dissolved-gas sample of a liquid that is not there
Winding resistance
Connection resistance
Partial discharge, which the table allows by construction
explanation: Dissolved gas, dielectric strength, acidity, and water are liquid-filled tests. A dry type has no oil sample to send out. The chapter still does not give a power-factor percent or a turns-ratio percent. Those numbers stay with the manufacturer or with the NETA table you are actually applying.

question: When the manufacturer is silent, NFPA 70B-2026 puts transformer electrical testing, other than the fluid sample, on:
choices: 60, 36, and 12 months
12, 12, and 6 months, the same row as the fluid sample and the infrared inspection
12, 6, and 3 months, the transfer-switch visual row
Before each use
explanation: Electrical testing, with the fluid sample excepted, is 60, 36, and 12 months when the manufacturer is silent. Fluid sampling stays on the shorter row. Infrared is not part of that electrical row. It has its own 12, 12, and 6 month row. Liquid-filled units still get the fluid tests. Dry types do not.

question: NFPA 70B-2026 inspection of a liquid-filled transformer includes level, pressure, and relief devices. A dry type instead emphasizes:
choices: The same oil sample, because every transformer has fluid
Connections, cooling, grounding impedance, and the enclosure, without a fluid sample
Specific gravity of the windings
A transfer-switch bypass test
explanation: Connections, cooling, grounding impedance, and the enclosure are the common inspection. Level, pressure, and relief devices are the liquid-filled additions. A dry type has no fluid sample and no dissolved-gas test. No oil limit is printed.

question: Checking single-phase polarity by inductive kick: dc flows in the HV winding, and the voltmeter leads are moved to the adjacent LV leads. When the dc is broken, the pointer swings the opposite way. The polarity is:
choices: Additive
Reversed core magnetization, so retest
Cannot be determined with dc
Subtractive
explanation: In the inductive-kick method, a swing opposite to the first deflection means subtractive polarity, and a swing in the same direction means additive. Polarity matters mainly when you parallel or bank transformers.

question: You're ratio-testing a delta-wye transformer whose wye neutral isn't brought out, using a single-phase ratio set. How do you do it?
choices: Skip ratio. It cannot be done without the neutral
Short out one phase of the delta winding to create a virtual neutral, and measure phase by phase
Test line-to-line on both sides and divide by √3 on both
Ground one LV terminal and read to the tank
explanation: With no X0, you short one delta phase so the applied voltage appears across a single winding pair with no neutral shift, then move the short for each phase. The test code shows this connection for a delta HV with a wye LV whose neutral is inaccessible. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.2.2.B.3; ref. IEEE C57.12.90-2021, 7.1.4.

question: Before the ATS 7.2.2 insulation power-factor test on a liquid-filled transformer, how are the windings set up?
choices: Left open so the test set can read each terminal separately
Short-circuited on themselves (each winding's terminals jumpered together), with bushings in place and windings under liquid
Grounded through the neutral bushing only
Energized at rated voltage
explanation: Shorting each winding keeps winding inductance out of the measurement, so you read the insulation alone. The test code also wants bushings installed, windings immersed, and a temperature between 10 °C and 40 °C, as close to 20 °C as practical. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.2.2.B.4; ref. IEEE C57.12.90-2021, 10.10.1.

question: Running an insulation power-factor test on a liquid-filled transformer winding, the test voltage should not exceed:
choices: Rated line-to-line voltage
Half the winding's low-frequency test voltage, or 10 kV, whichever is lower
Twice the operating voltage
1000 V for every winding
explanation: The cap is half the applied (low-frequency) test level for that winding or 10 kV, whichever is lower. So a low-voltage winding gets a lower test voltage than the HV winding. The 1000 V cap is the dry-type rule, not this one. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.2.2.B.4; ref. IEEE C57.12.90-2021, 10.10.3.

question: A dry-type transformer with a 13.8 kV primary gets an insulation power-factor test. The applied voltage should be limited to:
choices: 10 kV, the same as a liquid-filled unit
The winding's operating voltage to ground or 1000 V, whichever is lower, which here is 1000 V
Half the BIL
explanation: Dry-type units get a much lower ceiling than liquid-filled units: operating voltage to ground or 1000 V, whichever is lower. Using the liquid-filled 10 kV practice on a dry-type unit is the classic mistake. Source: IEEE C57.12.91-2020, 10.9.4.

question: You power-factor test a dry-type transformer. What's the most useful way to judge the result?
choices: Comparison with the factory value and with earlier field tests, since no standard pass/fail values have been set for dry types
The same 0.5% limit used for mineral-oil transformers
Anything under 5% passes
A single reading is decisive, so trending is unnecessary
explanation: The test code says standard dry-type power-factor values have not been established, because power factor has shown little relation to dielectric withstand. Trend against the factory baseline and earlier results rather than a fixed number. Source: IEEE C57.12.91-2020, 10.9.5 (note).

question: A 12,470 V delta to 480Y/277 V transformer is on nominal tap. When a delta winding is tested against its matching wye phase-to-neutral winding, the expected ratio is about:
explanation: On a wye winding, the ratio is judged against phase-to-neutral voltage, which is line-to-line divided by √3. 12,470 / 277 ≈ 45.0. Dividing by 480 (26.0) is the common error for delta-wye units.

question: On a TTR test, the calculated ratio is 45.02, and one phase measures 45.40. That phase is:
choices: About 0.84% off, outside the 0.5% tolerance, so investigate
About 0.08% off, acceptable
About 0.38% off, acceptable
About 8.4% off, a shorted turn for certain
explanation: (45.40 − 45.02) / 45.02 × 100 ≈ 0.84%. The guide's voltage-ratio tolerance is 0.5% of the nameplate value, so this phase needs investigation.

question: A three-legged core-form transformer gives a low-high-low excitation-current pattern instead of the expected high-low-high. Before suspecting a winding fault, check:
choices: Only the oil dielectric strength
Whether the tank was grounded to the station grid
The test protocol, for example whether the third terminal of a delta winding was grounded or whether the wye neutral was accessible
The ambient temperature correction
explanation: On a three-legged core, the outer phases normally read high and the center phase low. The guide lists an inverted pattern as a result of not following the usual test connections, an inaccessible high-side wye neutral, or an ungrounded third delta terminal. It is also normal for a four-legged core.

question: You plan to run winding resistance, excitation current, SFRA, and TTR on the same transformer, with no demagnetizing step. What order works best?
choices: Run excitation, FRA, and TTR first and winding resistance last, because the dc test magnetizes the core
Run winding resistance first so the core is saturated for the other tests
Order does not matter
Run winding resistance between each of the other tests
explanation: Dc winding-resistance current leaves residual magnetism that distorts excitation current and frequency response. Either demagnetize after the resistance test or put it at the end of the sequence. Source: IEEE C57.152-2025, 7.2.7.1 (note).

question: Per-phase leakage reactance results on a three-phase transformer are 10.0%, 10.1%, and 10.6%. The 10.6% phase is:
choices: Within 3% of the average, acceptable
Judged only against nameplate, not the average
Acceptable, since leakage reactance has no field limit
About 3.6% above the three-phase average, outside the 3% band, so investigate
explanation: The average is (10.0 + 10.1 + 10.6) / 3 ≈ 10.23%. 10.6 / 10.23 ≈ 1.036, which is 3.6% high. Per-phase results should sit within 3% of the three-phase average. A deviation that size can point to winding movement. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.2.2.D.10; ref. IEEE C57.152-2025, 7.2.12.1.5.

question: A 138 kV mineral-oil power transformer tests 0.7% insulation power factor, corrected to 20 °C. How do you read that?
choices: Normal for a new unit
Over the serviceability limit, so remove it from service now
Not comparable, since mineral oil has no published limit
Above the new or normal limit but under the 1.0% serviceability limit, so do more testing and investigation, and trend it
explanation: For mineral-oil units below 230 kV, the guide gives 0.5% as the new or normal limit and 1.0% as the serviceability limit, both at 20 °C. Results between those two call for added testing to make sure the condition is not getting worse.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.2.2.D.4 and Table 100.3; ref. IEEE C57.152-2025, 7.2.14.8

question: A condenser bushing's C1 power factor has doubled since its initial test. What should happen?
choices: Test it more often or remove it from service. Removal is called for if it reaches three times the initial value
Ignore it, since only capacitance matters on condenser bushings
Remove it only if it reaches ten times initial
Correct the reading to 20 °C and stop trending
explanation: A rise to 1.5 to 2 times the initial power factor means either more frequent testing or removal. Tripling means removal. Any bushing whose power factor keeps climbing should be scheduled out of service and the manufacturer consulted. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.2.2.D.5; ref. IEEE C57.152-2025, 7.3.4.1.

question: A solid (bulk) bushing with no test or voltage tap is mounted on the transformer. How do you assess it?
choices: A C1/C2 power-factor test through the tap
A hot collar test, judged on watt loss, with about 0.1 W as the generally accepted limit
A tip-up test at 10 kV through the tap
Insulation resistance at 15 kV
explanation: With no tap there is no C1/C2 measurement. A hot collar energizes a band around the porcelain with the conductor grounded, and you compare watt loss (about 0.1 W is the common limit) and current between similar bushings. It can also find cracks or a low oil level. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.2.2.D.5; ref. IEEE C57.152-2025, 7.3.4.1 and 7.3.4.4.

question: ATS has you evaluate dissolved-gas results against the guide for mineral oil. That guide is used to interpret:
choices: Dissolved gases in transformer oil
CT knee-point markers
VLF withstand voltage
Breaker instantaneous tolerance
explanation: ATS 7.2.2.D.15 says to evaluate dissolved-gas results in accordance with IEEE C57.104. The guide is about gases in mineral oil. It is not the CT excitation guide, the VLF cable guide, or the breaker instantaneous table.

question: A mineral-oil dissolved-gas result shows acetylene, with ethylene also up. Acetylene is the marker for:
choices: Cold cellulose drying
Arcing, or a very hot fault, rather than a calm thermal aging story
A normal new-oil baseline with no follow-up
A CT polarity error
explanation: Acetylene is produced by arcing in oil or paper at very high temperature. Ethylene tracks hotter heating of the oil or paper. Hydrogen can rise along with acetylene, so a low hydrogen number does not cancel the acetylene. ATS 7.2.2.D.15 says to evaluate the sample under that guide.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.2.2.D.15; ref. IEEE C57.104-2019, clause 6.2.1

question: When you plot a mineral-oil DGA result on Duval Triangle 1, which three gases set the point?
choices: Hydrogen, carbon monoxide, and carbon dioxide
Methane, ethylene, and acetylene
Oxygen, nitrogen, and moisture
Furan, acid number, and color
explanation: The triangle uses methane for lower-energy heating, ethylene for hotter faults, and acetylene for arcing. Hydrogen is interpreted with the other gases, but it is not a side of that triangle. ATS 7.2.2.D.15 sends the sample to this guide.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.2.2.D.15; ref. IEEE C57.104-2019, clause 6.2.3

question: In a mineral-oil transformer, at what fault temperature does acetylene become an important product?
choices: At ordinary service temperature
Only as the fault temperature nears 1000 °C
Whenever the oil is new
Only in the nitrogen blanket
explanation: Acetylene shows up in a meaningful amount only as the fault temperature gets up near 1000 °C. That point is in the text that opens clause 4. Methane, ethane, and ethylene show up with lower heating. A story that never reaches that temperature is not an acetylene story.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.2.2.D.15; ref. IEEE C57.104-2019, opening of clause 4

question: Carbon monoxide and carbon dioxide stand out on a mineral-oil DGA. They point toward:
choices: Heating of cellulose or of the insulating liquid
A reversed CT
A low power factor on the bushing tap only
Partial discharge with no other possibility
explanation: The carbon oxides are the cellulose and liquid-heating gases. Hydrogen is the partial-discharge and stray-gassing gas. Do not read a CO rise as a turns-ratio failure. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.2.2.D.15; ref. IEEE C57.104-2019, clause 6.2.1.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.2.2.D.15; ref. IEEE C57.104-2019, clause 6.2.1

question: A dissolved-gas result matches none of the Rogers-ratio cases, even though combustible gas is high. What does that tell you?
choices: The transformer is normal because it missed the table
The Rogers method simply did not identify a fault type
Acetylene must be ignored
The oil is ester, so mineral-oil rules do not apply
explanation: Rogers ratios miss a substantial share of real results because the ratios fall outside every case. That is a limit of the method, not a clean bill of health. Use another method in the guide, and still treat a rising trend as real.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.2.2.D.15; ref. IEEE C57.104-2019, clause 6.2.2

question: A DGA sample was exposed to air before analysis. What does the result tend to show?
choices: A large gain of acetylene
Loss of hydrogen, often with oxygen and nitrogen up
A perfect Duval triangle
No change, because hydrogen is not soluble
explanation: Hydrogen leaves the oil when the sample sees air. Oxygen and nitrogen come in. A sudden drop in hydrogen with a high oxygen-to-nitrogen ratio on a sealed transformer is a sampling problem until proved otherwise. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.2.2.B.15; ref. IEEE C57.104-2019, clause 5.1.4.1.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.2.2.B.15; ref. IEEE C57.104-2019, clause 5.1.4.1

question: Someone works out a yearly gassing rate from just two DGA samples. How good is that?
choices: The preferred and sufficient method
A weak way to judge gassing, because normal scatter can dominate two points
Required before any Duval triangle
A substitute for the oil power-factor test
explanation: The guide wants a rate that survives ordinary sample-to-sample noise, which is why it uses more than one pair of bottles. A single jump still gets attention. It does not, by itself, prove the rate.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.2.2.D.15; ref. IEEE C57.104-2019, clause 6

question: Combustible gas on a transformer DGA is high but stable. What should you still keep in mind?
choices: The level never matters
Rising levels are the greater concern, and the fault type matters as well as the level
Acetylene is required before any action
The sample can be left open overnight
explanation: A high stable number and a number that is climbing are not the same story. The kind of fault matters too. Air exposure, which drops hydrogen, can fake a falling trend, so the sample has to be real before the rate is.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.2.2.D.15; ref. IEEE C57.104-2019, clause 6

question: The first-ever DGA on a natural-ester transformer with no sample history comes back. The lab applied mineral-oil C57.104 limits and a standard Duval triangle, and both flag a fault. What should you do next?
choices: Accept the flag; the gases are the same as mineral oil, so the mineral-oil method is the right one
Ignore DGA on ester units, since it doesn’t apply
Re-screen on C57.155 Table 1 for this ester or local thresholds; if still over, confirm and trend
Retrofill with mineral oil so C57.104 applies
explanation: Esters make the same fault gases as mineral oil, but in different ratios and amounts, so an unmodified mineral-oil method isn’t reliable. With no history, C57.155 compares a first sample with its Table 1 percentile values for that fluid, or with local thresholds, and calls for a confirmation sample when they’re exceeded. Then trend it. Ratio and triangle methods only help once gases are above minimum levels, and Annex G uses triangle regions drawn for ester liquids. ATS names C57.104 because it assumes mineral oil.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.2.2.D.15; ref. IEEE C57.155-2014, clauses 4.1, 6.1 and Table 1, 6.3, and Annex G. Mineral-oil DGA remains IEEE C57.104-2019.

question: You are power-factor testing transformer bushings on a cold morning. Ambient is 6 °C and top oil is 30 °C. Which approach fits bushing test guidance?
choices: Use 6 °C for correction
Estimate bushing temperature as about 18 °C, the average of ambient and top oil, and correct to 20 °C
Use 30 °C for correction
Skip correction for bushings
explanation: For a bushing mounted in a transformer, its temperature is approximated as the average of ambient air and top-oil temperature: (6 + 30) / 2 = 18 °C. Results are then corrected to the 20 °C base. Do not test bushings below freezing, since ice can hide a bad bushing. Source: IEEE C57.19.100-2025, 10.4.1.

question: IEEE C57.91-2025 bases normal insulation life on what hottest-spot temperature and life expectancy for a 65 °C rise transformer?
choices: 110 °C and 180,000 h (about 20.5 years)
explanation: The standard life expectancy is 180,000 h (about 20.5 years) at a 110 °C hottest spot. That 110 °C is the 80 °C hottest-spot rise plus a 30 °C average ambient. Normal loss of life for 24 h at 110 °C is 0.0133%. Source: IEEE C57.91-2025, 5.3 and 9.3.1.

question: For a 65 °C rise power transformer, IEEE C57.91-2025 Table 10 recommends limits for loading above nameplate. Which set is right?
choices: Top oil 110 °C, hottest spot 180 °C, maximum load 200%
Top oil 105 °C, hottest spot 140 °C, maximum load 150%
Top oil 95 °C, hottest spot 120 °C, maximum load 130%
Top oil 120 °C, hottest spot 200 °C, maximum load 250%
explanation: Table 10 gives top oil 110 °C, conductor hottest spot 180 °C, and 200% maximum loading. Table 11 then gives hottest-spot limits by loading type: 120, 130, 140, and 180 °C. Source: IEEE C57.91-2025, 9.2.1, Tables 10 and 11.

question: A transformer will run hot for about two weeks while a parallel unit is out. In IEEE C57.91-2025 terms, that is which loading type, and what hottest-spot limit does Table 11 use for it?
choices: Planned loading beyond nameplate, 130 °C
Long-time emergency loading, 140 °C
Short-time emergency loading, 180 °C
Normal life loading, 120 °C
explanation: Long-time emergency loading comes from an outage lasting 24 h or more, is rare, and may persist for months. Table 11 uses 140 °C for it. Short-time emergency is under 24 h with a 180 °C limit. In both cases top oil should not exceed 110 °C. Source: IEEE C57.91-2025, 9.5, 9.6, and Table 11.

question: IEEE C57.91-2025 Table 2 gives a quick ambient adjustment. For an ONAN transformer with a 35 °C average daily ambient instead of 30 °C, the load should be lowered by about:
explanation: For ONAN, Table 2 is 1.5% of rating lower for each °C above 30 °C average ambient (and 1.0% higher for each °C below). 5 °C × 1.5% = 7.5%. The table is a quick approximation, not for actual planning limits. Source: IEEE C57.91-2025, 6.4 and Table 2.

question: Why does IEEE C57.91-2025 warn about top-oil temperatures above 105 °C on a 65 °C rise transformer?
choices: Oil turns to sludge instantly
Oil expansion may exceed the tank's capacity and operate the pressure relief device, expelling oil
Bushings flash over
Cooling fans stop
explanation: Above 105 °C top oil (65 °C rise over 40 °C ambient), oil expansion may exceed what the tank holds, building pressure that can operate the pressure relief device and expel oil. Lost oil can upset the preservation system or expose parts when it cools. Source: IEEE C57.91-2025, 4.1 i).

question: An operator wants to load a power transformer using the top-oil gauge alone. What does IEEE C57.91-2025 say?
choices: That's acceptable for normal life loading
Top oil alone should not be used; subtract the hottest-spot-to-top-oil gradient, corrected for load, from 110 °C to get the allowed oil temperature
Use top oil plus 10 °C
Use the winding gauge only
explanation: Top-oil temperature alone isn't a guide to loading. Use the full-load hottest-spot-to-top-oil gradient from factory tests (or an assumed value), correct it to actual load, and subtract it from 110 °C. Thermal lag also means temperatures take time to settle after a load change. Source: IEEE C57.91-2025, 9.3.3.

question: A bushing's power factor is trending up across several tests. Per IEEE C57.19.100-2025, what increase do some manufacturers consider significant?
choices: 10% above initial
1.5 to 2 times the initial reading
Any value above 0.5%
Only a doubling of capacitance
explanation: Some manufacturers treat a rise to 1.5 to 2 times the initial reading as significant. A bushing with a continuing rise should be investigated, tested more often, and considered for removal, with the manufacturer consulted. Source: IEEE C57.19.100-2025, 10.4.1.

question: A bushing tests at a questionable power factor at 38 °C. Per IEEE C57.19.100-2025, what should be done before condemning it?
choices: Condemn it if the corrected value is high
Let it cool to near 20 °C and retest, since correction factors are averages with error
Test it below freezing instead
Increase test voltage
explanation: Temperature correction factors are averages and carry error, which is smaller near 20 °C. A bushing with a questionable result at high temperature shouldn't be condemned until it cools near 20 °C and is retested. Source: IEEE C57.19.100-2025, 10.4.1.

question: For a standard 65 °C rise liquid-immersed transformer, IEEE C57.12.00-2021 limits average winding rise and hottest-spot winding rise over ambient at rated kVA to:
choices: 55 °C and 65 °C
65 °C and 80 °C
65 °C and 110 °C
80 °C and 110 °C
explanation: Average winding rise may not exceed 65 °C and hottest-spot winding rise may not exceed 80 °C at rated kVA, using the tap connection that gives the highest rise. Top-liquid rise near the top of the main tank is also limited to 65 °C. Source: IEEE C57.12.00-2021, 5.11.1.1 and 5.11.1.5.

question: A mineral-oil distribution transformer has a winding insulation power factor of 1.4% at 20 °C. How do ATS and MTS Table 100.3 treat it?
choices: Both fail it, since 0.5% is the mineral-oil limit
ATS: compare to prior results; MTS: 2.0% max
Both pass it, since the limit is 3.0%
ATS allows 2.0%; MTS requires 0.5%
explanation: The ATS table gives numbers only for power transformers, regulators, and reactors. Note 2 says distribution transformers compare with prior results. MTS gives distribution and apparatus transformers 2.0% for mineral oil. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 Table 100.3 note 2; ANSI/NETA MTS-2023 Table 100.3.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 Table 100.3 note 2; ANSI/NETA MTS-2023 Table 100.3

question: A liquid-filled transformer with a 13.8 kV winding is megger tested at acceptance and again at maintenance. How do the ATS and MTS Table 100.5 minimums compare?
choices: MTS allows half the ATS value
The same: 5000 V and 5000 MΩ
ATS uses 2500 V; MTS uses 5000 V
MTS has no table; it uses trending only
explanation: Both tables list 5000 V dc and 5000 MΩ for liquid-filled windings above 5 kV (25,000 MΩ for dry). ATS adds a note that natural-ester units read lower and are compared with factory or previous results. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 Table 100.5; ANSI/NETA MTS-2023 Table 100.5.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 Table 100.5; ANSI/NETA MTS-2023 Table 100.5

question: A pad-mount nameplate lists the high-voltage winding as 12470GrdY/7200. What does the GrdY tell you before you connect it?
choices: The winding can be reconnected delta for a 12,470 V ungrounded system
The neutral is fully insulated and may float
Reduced neutral-end insulation, for an effectively grounded system only
The winding is grounded through a resistor inside the tank
explanation: GrdY marks a wye winding with reduced insulation at the neutral end. It may be tied to the tank only where the neutral is effectively grounded. It is not a reconnectable delta winding and is not for an ungrounded system. Source: IEEE C57.12.00-2021, 5.12.3, Table 7 item (1)(d) and Table 8 item (2)(f).
reference: IEEE C57.12.00-2021, 5.12.3, Table 7 item (1)(d) and Table 8 item (2)(f)

question: A three-phase nameplate shows 2400/4160Y for one winding. That winding is:
choices: Delta on a 2,400 V system, or wye with no neutral out on 4,160 V
Permanently wye-connected with 2,400 V available from line to neutral
Rated 2,400 V on one tap and 4,160 V on another tap
Suitable only for a grounded 4,160 V wye system
explanation: The E/E1Y form means the same winding can be connected delta for E volts or wye for E1 volts with the neutral not brought out. 4160Y/2400, written the other way round, is the permanently wye form with a fully insulated neutral brought out. Source: IEEE C57.12.00-2021, 5.12.3, Table 8 items (2)(c) and (2)(d).

question: In the nameplate form E/E1Y, E1 is the wye line-to-line voltage. For a 7,200 V delta rating, what E1 would the nameplate show?
explanation: Table 7's notes define E1 as √3 times E. 7,200 × 1.732 ≈ 12,470 V. That is why 7200/12470Y and 12470GrdY/7200 pair up. Source: IEEE C57.12.00-2021, 5.12.3, Table 7 Notes 1 and 2.

question: A single-phase nameplate reads 240/120. Compared with a 120/240 winding, what does it allow?
choices: Full kVA from each 120 V half at the same time as full kVA at 240 V
Series or parallel connection only, with no center terminal
Operation at 120 V only, with 240 V as a test rating
Full kVA at 240 V, or three-wire with half kVA per 120 V half
explanation: 2E/E is a 2E-volt winding that carries full kVA between the outer terminals. As a three-wire service, each half (midpoint to an outer terminal) is limited to half the kVA. E/2E (120/240) can be paralleled for E or put in series for 2E. Source: IEEE C57.12.00-2021, 5.12.3, Table 7 items (1)(e) and (1)(f).

question: On a de-energized tap changer, the nameplate tap list runs 1 through 5 (or A through E). Which position gives the highest ratio of HV volts to LV volts?
choices: Tap 3, the middle position
Tap 1 (or A)
Tap 5 (or E)
Whichever tap is marked N
explanation: The standard assigns the numeral 1 or letter A to the voltage giving the maximum ratio of transformation. The ratio is HV volts divided by LV volts. N is the neutral position of a load tap changer, not of a de-energized tap changer. Source: IEEE C57.12.00-2021, 5.12.2, Table 6 note d.

question: For which transformers must the nameplate percent impedance be the tested value rather than a design value?
choices: Only single-phase units
Transformers rated 501 kVA and larger
Every transformer regardless of size
Only units with a BIL of 150 kV or more
explanation: Note e says %Z is given between each pair of windings, and for units of 501 kVA and larger it is the measured value. The voltage connection follows each %Z, and the kVA base is stated if there is more than one rating. Source: IEEE C57.12.00-2021, 5.12.2, Table 6 note e.

question: A 300 kVA unit with a 95 kV BIL high-voltage winding carries Nameplate A. Which item from a larger unit's Nameplate C will you NOT find on it?
choices: Percent impedance between windings
Tap voltages for the de-energized tap changer
Average winding temperature rise
Basic lightning impulse insulation levels (BIL)
explanation: Nameplate A is for units of 500 kVA or less with HV BIL under 150 kV, and its BIL row is blank. Nameplates B and C list BIL. Impedance, taps, and temperature rise are on all three. Source: IEEE C57.12.00-2021, 5.12.2 and Table 6.

question: A single-phase pole-type nameplate shows additive polarity. Which unit is that consistent with?
choices: A 100 kVA unit with a 7,200 V high-voltage winding
A 500 kVA unit with a 7,200 V high-voltage winding
A 100 kVA unit with a 13,800 V high-voltage winding
Any three-phase unit
explanation: Single-phase units of 200 kVA or less with HV of 8,660 V or less are additive. All other single-phase units are subtractive. Polarity applies to single-phase units. Three-phase units show a phasor diagram instead. Source: IEEE C57.12.00-2021, 5.7.1 and Table 6 rows 10 and 11.
reference: IEEE C57.12.00-2021, 5.7.1 and Table 6 rows 10 and 11

question: A nameplate is stamped 65 °C rise. Under the standard's usual service conditions, what is that rise measured above?
choices: The liquid temperature at the top of the tank
A fixed 20 °C reference
The ambient air, max 40 °C and 30 °C 24-hour average
The temperature of the hottest spot in the winding
explanation: 65 °C is the average winding rise over ambient. The hottest-spot rise allowed with it is 80 °C. The usual service conditions cap ambient at 40 °C and the 24-hour average at 30 °C. Source: IEEE C57.12.00-2021, 4.1.2.1 and 5.11.1.1.

question: On a sealed-tank transformer, the pressure-vacuum gauge reads zero every visit, in hot and cold weather and at all loads. What is the most likely meaning?
choices: The transformer is lightly loaded and healthy
The pressure relief device has been reset correctly
A leak in the gas space
The liquid level is too high for the season
explanation: A sealed tank keeps the gas plus liquid volume fixed, so the gauge should swing above and below zero as the liquid warms and cools. A reading stuck at zero points to a gas-space leak. Moisture can then get in, so a top sample for water is the next step. Source: Gill, Electrical Power Equipment Maintenance and Testing, 2nd ed., 4.5.2.2; IEEE C57.12.00-2021, 6.6.2.
reference: Gill, Electrical Power Equipment Maintenance and Testing, 2nd ed., 4.5.2.2; IEEE C57.12.00-2021, 6.6.2

question: During acceptance testing of a liquid-filled transformer, what does ATS want done with the temperature and liquid-level indicators?
choices: Check the settings against the spec, then operate the alarm and trip circuits
Record the dial readings only; circuits are checked by the owner
Replace the indicators with calibrated units
Bypass the trip contacts so the unit cannot trip during energization
explanation: ATS 7.2.2 asks for both: settings on temperature and level indicators as specified, and a check that their alarm, control, and trip circuits really operate. The same check covers the pressure relief device, gas accumulator, and fault-pressure relay. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025, 7.2.2.A.9 and A.10; ANSI/NETA MTS-2023, 7.2.2.A.6.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025, 7.2.2.A.9 and A.10; ANSI/NETA MTS-2023, 7.2.2.A.6

question: A Nameplate C transformer has a gas cushion above the oil. Which nameplate data lets you judge the liquid-level gauge reading on a hot afternoon?
choices: The percent impedance and the kVA base it was measured on
The BIL of each winding and the neutral
The untanking weight of the core and coils
The 25 °C level below the flange and the change per 10 °C
explanation: Note m puts the 25 °C level and the change per 10 °C on the nameplate for units with a gas cushion. Correct the expected level for today's liquid temperature before calling it low or high. Source: IEEE C57.12.00-2021, 5.12.2, Table 6 row 23 and note m.
reference: IEEE C57.12.00-2021, 5.12.2, Table 6 row 23 and note m

question: On a nitrogen-blanketed transformer, the MTS visual inspection includes which pressure check?
choices: Verify the blanket is at atmospheric pressure
Verify positive pressure is maintained on the gas blanket
Vent the blanket before each inspection
Verify a slight vacuum is held on the gas space
explanation: Both ATS and MTS list verifying positive pressure on gas-blanketed transformers. A blanket that has dropped to zero can let in air and moisture. MTS also offers an optional oxygen-percentage check of the blanket. Source: ANSI/NETA MTS-2023, 7.2.2.A.10 and B.12; ANSI/NETA ATS-2025, 7.2.2.A.15.
reference: ANSI/NETA MTS-2023, 7.2.2.A.10 and B.12; ANSI/NETA ATS-2025, 7.2.2.A.15

question: A delta-wye step-down transformer is built to the IEEE standard angular displacement. The low-voltage phase-to-neutral voltages relative to the high-voltage ones:
choices: Lead by 30°
Lag by 30°
Are in phase (0°)
Lag by 60°
explanation: For delta-wye and wye-delta three-phase units, the standard displacement has the low-voltage side lagging the high-voltage side by 30°. Delta-delta and wye-wye units are 0°. The nameplate phasor diagram shows it. Source: IEEE C57.12.00-2021, 5.7.2.

question: A mill needs to serve a two-phase furnace from a three-phase 13.8 kV supply. Which transformer arrangement does IEEE C57.12.00 describe for that conversion?
choices: A Scott-connected or T-connected transformer, which is the arrangement given for converting a three-phase supply to two-phase, or the reverse
A standard delta-wye distribution transformer, which inherently produces a two-phase output
An autotransformer with a midtap, which is the only arrangement C57.12.00 allows for this service
A zig-zag grounding transformer, which converts three-phase power to two-phase power
explanation: IEEE C57.12.00 describes Scott-connected or T-connected transformers as the way to convert a three-phase supply to two-phase, or the reverse, and it also describes arrangements that can be used for three-phase to three-phase service. A ordinary delta-wye unit does not produce a two-phase output, and a zig-zag grounding transformer is not the arrangement the standard gives for this conversion. Source: IEEE C57.12.00-2021, 5.3.2 and 5.3.2.1.

question: A Category III power transformer will be applied on a system that can hold a through-fault for several seconds. The purchase specification is silent on short-circuit duration. What duration does IEEE C57.12.00 use as the limit unless the user specifies otherwise?
choices: Thirty cycles for every category, with no option for the user to specify a longer time
Ten seconds for Category III and IV, and two seconds only for Category I
There is no duration limit in C57.12.00; only impedance is specified
Two seconds for Category II, III, and IV units, unless the user specifies a different duration
explanation: For Category II, III, and IV transformers, IEEE C57.12.00 limits the duration of the defined short-circuit current to two seconds unless the user specifies otherwise. Category I uses a separate duration equation. If a longer fault time is expected in service, that needs to be specified rather than assumed. Source: IEEE C57.12.00-2021, 7.1.3.1.

question: A Category II transformer will sit on a feeder with automatic reclosing, so it can see more than one through-fault before it cools back to normal operating temperature. What capability does IEEE C57.12.00 require?
choices: Reclosing duty is never allowed; the transformer must cool to ambient between every fault
The transformer must ride through those repeated faults without first cooling back to normal temperature, as long as the total time does not exceed the single-event limit
Any number of recloses is allowed so long as each individual fault is shorter than 30 seconds
Only Category I units have a reclosing requirement; Category II and above are exempt
explanation: When a transformer is used on a circuit that can reclose, IEEE C57.12.00 requires units in all categories to ride through those repeated faults without first cooling back to normal temperature between events, as long as the total time does not exceed the single-event limit. That single-event limit is the one defined in 7.1.3.1. Source: IEEE C57.12.00-2021, 7.1.3.1.

question: A truck of unused natural-ester insulating liquid has just arrived. Which flash-point and fire-point values does IEEE C57.147-2018 treat as acceptable for that as-received shipment?
choices: The same limits used for conventional mineral oil, typically well below 200 C, may be applied without change
A minimum flash point of 275 C and a minimum fire point of 300 C, both by ASTM D92. Lower values suggest contamination with a lower-flash material such as conventional mineral oil
A fire point of 200 C is acceptable if the dielectric breakdown is high
Flash and fire points are not used for unused natural-ester receipts; only water content is checked
explanation: Natural esters have significantly higher flash and fire points than conventional mineral oil. ASTM D6871 sets unused natural-ester minima of 275 C flash point and 300 C fire point by D92 for liquid as received, and those same minima appear in Table 2 of the guide. Low values of either point indicate contamination with a lower-flash material such as conventional mineral oil. These D92 results are laboratory response data and are not, by themselves, a complete fire-risk assessment. Source: IEEE C57.147-2018, 4.10 and Table 2.

question: A lab applies the same absolute dissolved-water limit, in mg/kg, that it uses for mineral oil to a natural-ester sample and flags the ester as wet. How should you read that comparison?
choices: Natural esters hold much less water than mineral oil, so a mineral-oil ppm limit is conservative and should be enforced as written

Absolute milligram-per-kilogram limits written for mineral oil are not applicable. Natural esters hold about 15 to 20 times as much water at saturation at room temperature, and the effect on dielectric strength tracks percent of saturation, which is similar for both liquids
Water content has no effect on the dielectric strength of a natural ester, so the reading can be ignored
The two liquids have the same saturation values at every temperature, so the same absolute limit may be used
explanation: Dissolved-water limits written for mineral oil do not transfer to natural esters. Dielectric strength versus percent of saturation tracks essentially the same curve for both liquids, so comparing by relative saturation is the fair approach. Natural ester holds far more water in solution at a given temperature, so a mineral-oil ppm cap would be either too loose or too tight if it were applied unchanged. Source: IEEE C57.147-2018, 4.16 and Annex B.

question: An owner wants to put a natural-ester transformer on a free-breathing conservator with no bladder. What does IEEE C57.147-2018 say about that arrangement?
choices: Natural esters are more oxidation-resistant than mineral oil, so a free-breathing conservator is preferred
Oxidation of a natural ester forms the same carbonaceous sludge as mineral oil and is harmless in a breathing tank
A bladderless conservator is acceptable if the fire point remains above 200 C

Natural esters are not as oxidation-resistant as mineral oil, so free-breathing equipment, including a bladderless conservator, is not recommended. Continuous, long-term exchange of air should be avoided, especially at operating temperature
explanation: Natural esters oxidize more readily than mineral oil, so the guide does not recommend free-breathing tanks or conservators without a bladder (or an equivalent air-exclusion scheme). Avoid leaving the liquid open to an unlimited air exchange for long periods, especially while it is at operating temperature. Oxidation in natural ester shows up first as a rise in viscosity. Source: IEEE C57.147-2018, 4.15.

question: In-service natural-ester viscosity has climbed well above the original value, while the unit has had long exposure to air in the head space. What does that trend most likely indicate?
choices: Excessive polymerization from oxidation, typically from abnormal exposure to air and heat. Natural esters are already more viscous than mineral oil, and a further rise can reduce cooling capability
A viscosity increase is the expected, harmless result of ester stray gassing and can be ignored
Rising viscosity means the liquid is being diluted with mineral oil and the fire point will go up
Viscosity is not used to judge natural esters, so the trend has no maintenance meaning
explanation: Natural esters are typically more viscous than mineral oil. Viscosity governs heat transfer and also how the liquid moves through processing equipment. A continual exchange of air in the headspace over several years can raise viscosity if the free surface of the liquid is left open to that air. That thickening can weaken the insulation system's dielectric strength. Source: IEEE C57.147-2018, 4.9 and 4.15.

question: Unused natural ester has been processed into a new 138 kV transformer and has stood for the required time. Before the unit is energized, which dissolved-water limits does IEEE C57.147-2018 Table 3 give, by voltage class?
choices: A single 200 mg/kg as-received shipment limit applies after the unit is filled, at every voltage class
Water is not limited after filling; only color and visual condition are checked
A maximum of 300 mg/kg at 69 kV and below, 150 mg/kg above 69 kV and below 230 kV, and 100 mg/kg at 230 kV and above. The fire point must still be at least 300 C
The limit is 450 mg/kg at every voltage class, which is the in-service figure for continued use
explanation: Table 3 gives acceptance limits for unused natural ester received in new equipment, or after filling on site, prior to energization. Dissolved water by ASTM D1533 is limited to 300 mg/kg at 69 kV and below, 150 mg/kg above 69 kV and below 230 kV, and 100 mg/kg at 230 kV and above. The fire point minimum remains 300 C in every class. Those after-fill water numbers are tighter than the 200 mg/kg as-received shipment limit in Table 2, which applies before the mandatory processing of bulk liquid. In-service continued-use water limits in Table 4 are higher still (450 / 350 / 200 mg/kg). Source: IEEE C57.147-2018, Table 3 and Clause 7.

question: You are judging a dielectric-breakdown test on unused natural ester just after a new transformer was filled, using ASTM D1816 with a 1 mm gap. Which minima does Table 3 of IEEE C57.147-2018 require by voltage class?
choices: 20 kV in every class, which is the as-received shipment minimum at a 1 mm gap
40 kV in every class, which is an in-service continued-use figure at a 2 mm gap
25 kV at 69 kV and below, 30 kV above 69 kV and below 230 kV, and 35 kV at 230 kV and above
There is no voltage-class distinction; a single 35 kV floor applies at 1 mm after filling
explanation: Table 3, for unused liquid in new equipment prior to energization, sets ASTM D1816 1 mm-gap minima of 25 kV, 30 kV, and 35 kV for the three voltage classes, and 2 mm-gap minima of 45 kV, 55 kV, and 60 kV. Those are higher than the as-received shipment minima in Table 2 (20 kV at 1 mm and 35 kV at 2 mm). In-service continued-use minima in Table 4 are lower than the after-fill values (23 / 28 / 30 kV at 1 mm). Source: IEEE C57.147-2018, Table 3.

question: A natural-ester transformer has just been filled and the vacuum has been broken. The superintendent wants to high-potential the unit immediately, the way the crew does after a mineral-oil fill. What standing-time guidance does IEEE C57.147-2018 give?
choices: Natural esters generally take significantly longer to impregnate cellulose than mineral oil. If the manufacturer has no better figure, consider at least 8 hours (24 hours preferred) for a distribution transformer and at least 24 hours, or more, for a power transformer, and run any circulating pumps for at least several hours of that time
Natural esters impregnate cellulose faster than mineral oil, so the usual mineral-oil wait can be shortened
Energization may begin as soon as the tank is full, because ester viscosity does not affect impregnation
A 15-minute stand is enough at any voltage class if the fire point is 300 C
explanation: After a fill, most manufacturers advise a longer wait, once vacuum is broken, before energizing or running a high-voltage test, than the wait used with mineral oil. A cautious alternative is to postpone energizing or testing until the unit has returned to ambient temperature. The guide also gives minimum sit times of 8 h, with 24 h preferred, for distribution units, and at least 24 h for power units, with pumps run for several hours when they are fitted. Source: IEEE C57.147-2018, Clause 7.

question: A less-flammable natural-ester transformer, installed to keep a 300 C fire-point rating, is sampled in service and the fire point comes back below 300 C. What should you do?
choices: A fire point below 300 C is normal after a few months in service and needs no follow-up
The 300 C floor applies only to unused liquid in drums and does not apply after the transformer is filled
Drop the fire-point test from the in-service screen; only dielectric breakdown is used on service-aged esters
Treat a fire point under 300 C as evidence of leftover mineral oil and investigate. For installations that must keep a less-flammable or K-class rating, a fire point under 300 C is not acceptable
explanation: Table 4 lists an optional in-service fire-point minimum of 300 C in every voltage class. After a retrofit fill, residual mineral oil can pull the ester's fire point down. For transformers that must keep a less-flammable rating, or that are otherwise known to require a 300 C fire point, a sample below 300 C is a sign of leftover mineral oil and should be investigated. Dedicated handling equipment, or a flush equal to at least 5% of the ester charge, is the preferred way to avoid that contamination when equipment has also been used on mineral oil.
