Source: IEEE C57.147-2018, Table 4 note d and 6.5 note 1.
reference: IEEE C57.147-2018, Table 4 note d and 6.5 note 1

question: A storage tank of natural ester has to be warmed before it can be pumped. What heater limits does IEEE C57.147-2018 give to avoid scorching the liquid?
choices: Any immersion heater is acceptable; natural esters cannot be scorched

Limit surface loading to 1.9 W/cm2 (that is 12 W/in2) or less, and keep the heater face at 100 C or less. Scorching shows up as a high dissipation factor, a darkened liquid, a burnt odor, or charred residue on the element
Watt density may go to 10 W/cm2 as long as the bulk liquid stays under 80 C
The only limit is a 150 C heater surface; watt density is not restricted
explanation: If the liquid must be heated, choose the heater carefully. To avoid scorching, keep surface loading at or below 1.9 W/cm2 (that is 12 W/in2) and keep the heater face at 100 C or less. Overheating can leave a burnt odor and charred residue on the element. Those limits matter because a natural ester's pour point is higher than mineral oil, so heating is sometimes needed for handling. Source: IEEE C57.147-2018, 6.4.1.

question: You are filling a transformer with natural ester through filter hoses. What static-charge precaution does IEEE C57.147-2018 require, and how should handling equipment be managed if it has also been used on mineral oil?
choices: Grounding is unnecessary during an ester fill because the liquid cannot hold a static charge

Ground all accessible bushing terminals, the tank, and the filtering equipment including the hoses, because liquid moving through filter paper or ungrounded hoses can charge the windings. Prefer equipment used only on natural ester; otherwise flush with a volume equal to at least 5% of the ester charge so leftover mineral oil does not pull the fire point down
Mineral-oil residual in hoses is harmless to the fire point, so mixed-service equipment needs no flush
Only the pump frame needs a ground; hoses and bushings may be left floating
explanation: Insulating liquids, including natural esters, can pick up an electrostatic charge when they pass through filter papers or ungrounded or unbonded hoses, and that charge can transfer to the windings. Under some conditions the voltage may be hazardous. The guide requires that all externally accessible bushing terminals, the tank, and the liquid-filtering equipment, including hoses, be properly grounded during filling. Pumps and lines must also be grounded during transfer. Dedicated handling equipment is preferred when a 300 C fire point must be kept; otherwise flush the equipment with a volume equal to at least 5% of the ester charge. Do not exceed the tank vacuum limit on the nameplate. Source: IEEE C57.147-2018, 6.4.1 warning, 6.5 warning and note 1, and 6.5 caution.
reference: IEEE C57.147-2018, 6.4.1 warning, 6.5 warning and note 1, and 6.5 caution

question: You need a representative sample of mineral oil or a similar insulating liquid whose specific gravity is less than 1, taken from a drum or a large storage tank. Where does ASTM D923-07 tell you to take that sample, unless a different location is specified?
choices: Always from the surface layer, because water floats on every insulating liquid
Always from mid-depth, because top and bottom samples are never representative
From the bottom only when specific gravity is greater than 1

From the bottom. In drums, cans, and small vessels the device should draw about 3 mm off the floor; in large vessels, tank trucks, and tank cars, within 13 mm of the floor. Water and some other impurities collect there when specific gravity is less than 1
explanation: When specific gravity is less than 1, water and some other impurities tend to settle at or near the floor, so those liquids are sampled from the bottom unless otherwise specified. The sampling device is designed to draw 3 mm off the floor in drums, cans, and small vessels, and within 13 mm of the floor in large vessels, tank trucks, and tank cars. Liquids with specific gravity greater than 1 are sampled from the surface layer. New liquid in containers should be left undisturbed at least 8 hours before sampling when a referee test is required. Source: ASTM D923-07, 3.1.1.1, 5.4.3, 5.4.4, and 5.4.2.

question: A crew is about to draw an oil sample from an energized instrument transformer that has only a small oil volume. What mandatory limits does ASTM D923-07 place on that work?
choices: Do not sample energized instrument transformers such as CTs and PTs, and do not sample any energized apparatus that has only a small volume of oil, especially if oil would have to be added to keep the insulation's electric strength. An energized unit that is sampled must be under positive pressure at the sample valve so air is not drawn in
Energized CTs and PTs may be sampled freely as long as the bottle is clean
A drain plug is an acceptable sampling point on energized gear
Positive pressure at the outlet is optional; a slight vacuum at the valve is acceptable
explanation: Mandatory conditions include: the energized apparatus must have positive pressure at the sampling outlet so an air bubble is not introduced; do not sample energized equipment that holds only a small volume of oil, especially if oil must be added to maintain electric strength; maintain the liquid level so the insulation's electric strength is not reduced; do not sample if only a drain plug is provided, because flow is hard to control; and do not draw samples from energized instrument transformers such as CTs and PTs. Source: ASTM D923-07, 5.1.1 through 5.1.5 and 7.2.

question: A dissolved-gas and water sample is needed from a transformer, and the only containers on the truck are clear glass bottles and soldered tin cans. The relative humidity is above 50%, and the oil is colder than the air. What sampling guidance from ASTM D923-07 should you apply?
choices: Any clean glass bottle is equivalent to a syringe for dissolved-gas work, and humidity does not matter
Soldered-seam metal cans are the preferred dissolved-gas container

Prefer a glass syringe or a stainless-steel cylinder for dissolved-gas and water work; bottles and ordinary cans let gases escape or let air in. It is undesirable to take atmosphere-exposed samples when humidity exceeds 50%, or in rain or snow, and the liquid should be at least as warm as the air so the sample does not pick up condensed moisture
The oil should be colder than the air so that moisture will condense in the bottle and be easy to see
explanation: Syringes, or stainless-steel cylinders, are the preferred devices for dissolved-gas and water samples. If bottles or cans are used, gases can escape or environmental gases can enter and change the results. Soldered seams can leave a residue that contaminates the sample. When the liquid may be colder than the air, as on large outdoor tanks, it is undesirable to collect atmosphere-exposed samples if relative humidity exceeds 50%, or in rain or snow. In general, the liquid should be equal to or warmer than the surrounding air so condensed moisture is not absorbed, especially in a humid atmosphere. Clear bottles help you see impurities; amber bottles, or storage in the dark, protect samples from light when that matters. Source: ASTM D923-07, 5.2.3, 5.4.1, 6.4 notes 1 and 2, 6.5, and 6.6.

question: A power transformer has just been through a close-in through-fault, and the lockout has operated. Besides the usual power-factor, TTR, excitation, and leakage-reactance tests, when does the NETA Transformer Handbook's SFRA article say a sweep-frequency response test is particularly useful?
choices: After a fault or protection trip, to help judge the nature and extent of any mechanical damage. It is also used in a condition assessment, especially if the unit has seen short circuits over time, and for comparison before and after a relocation
SFRA is useful only on a brand-new unit at the factory and has no field role after a through-fault
SFRA replaces dissolved-gas analysis and is the only test needed after a trip
SFRA should be delayed until the next scheduled outage, because a recent fault makes the traces unreadable
explanation: The handbook article on sweep-frequency response analysis places the test among condition-assessment tools that can provide corroborative evidence before an expensive decision. It is used when investigating after a fault or a protection trip, to help judge the nature and extent of any damage; during a condition assessment, including on a unit that has seen short circuits over time and apparently withstood them, to look for possible damage and remaining short-circuit capability; and for comparisons taken before a move and after it, which should show any mechanical movement. New and refurbished units are also tested to obtain fingerprint traces, and sister units of similar design can be used as references. Source: Locarno, Tully, and Wilson, The Detection of Mechanical Damage in Power Transformers Using the Sweep Frequency Response Analysis Method, in NETA Transformer Handbook, Vol. 1.
reference: Locarno, Tully, and Wilson, The Detection of Mechanical Damage in Power Transformers Using the Sweep Frequency Response Analysis Method, in NETA Transformer Handbook, Vol. 1

question: An SFRA trace on a relocated transformer differs from the trace taken before the move, while power factor and ratio still look acceptable. What kind of problem is the handbook's SFRA article aimed at, and how should the trace be used?
choices: A changed SFRA trace is conclusive proof of winding insulation failure, even if every other test is unchanged
SFRA is only sensitive to oil moisture and cannot show mechanical movement

The method is aimed at mechanical damage such as winding movement, radial buckling, or axial deformation from shipping or short-circuit forces, and at loss of core grounds. Treat it as corroborative evidence alongside the other diagnostic tests, not as a stand-alone condemnation
If power factor is still acceptable, a changed SFRA trace can be ignored
explanation: Power transformers are specified to withstand shipping forces and in-service short circuits. The most severe service forces come from close-in faults, faults in a load-tap changer, and, for a generator transformer, unsynchronized energization. Those forces can cause radial buckling or axial deformation, and inadequate restraints during transport can move the core and windings. The article presents SFRA as a method focused on that mechanical condition, used with power factor, exciting current, turns ratio, leakage reactance, and other diagnostics, and as corroborative evidence prior to an expensive consequential decision, not as a lone go/no-go test. Source: Locarno, Tully, and Wilson, The Detection of Mechanical Damage in Power Transformers Using the Sweep Frequency Response Analysis Method, in NETA Transformer Handbook, Vol. 1.
reference: Locarno, Tully, and Wilson, The Detection of Mechanical Damage in Power Transformers Using the Sweep Frequency Response Analysis Method, in NETA Transformer Handbook, Vol. 1

question: A manufacturer offers only a sister-unit SFRA fingerprint, not a trace from the exact transformer you are commissioning. Is that usable according to the handbook article?
choices: Only a factory trace from the exact serial number is ever usable; a sister-unit reference has no value
Sister-unit comparisons are valid only for oil screen tests, not for SFRA
Yes. Traces from sister units of similar design can be used as references, and new or refurbished units are also tested to obtain fingerprint values for later comparison
Fingerprints are taken only after the first in-service fault, never on a new or refurbished unit
explanation: Testing is carried out on new and refurbished units to obtain fingerprint values for later reference. Test results on sister units of similar design can also be used as references. Manufacturers also use the method as a quality check by comparing the response of units built to the same design. Those comparisons are in addition to the before-and-after relocation and after-fault uses of the test. Source: Locarno, Tully, and Wilson, The Detection of Mechanical Damage in Power Transformers Using the Sweep Frequency Response Analysis Method, in NETA Transformer Handbook, Vol. 1.
reference: Locarno, Tully, and Wilson, The Detection of Mechanical Damage in Power Transformers Using the Sweep Frequency Response Analysis Method, in NETA Transformer Handbook, Vol. 1
